Planned Experiments: (1) Robot manipulation benchmarks (RLBench, MetaWorld) measuring recovery rate after induced perturbations across failure type categories; (2) Few-shot adaptation tasks comparing correction specificity against ThinkAct and reflexion-style baselines; (3) Ablations isolating the contrastive retrieval component vs. naive retry; (4) Human evaluation of generated failure diagnoses for interpretability.

title: HierarchicalThink: Multi-Granularity Visual Latent Planning with Temporal Abstraction for Long-Horizon Manipulation
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning into a single visual plan latent, which struggles to capture multi-scale temporal structure in long-horizon tasks requiring both strategic (task-level) and tactical (motion-level) planning simultaneously. A single latent vector conflates minutes-long goal intentions with second-level motion primitives, limiting expressiveness for complex manipulation sequences.

Method: We propose HierarchicalThink, extending ThinkAct with a two-level visual latent planning hierarchy. A high-level LLM generates coarse subgoal sequences (e.g., 'grasp handle → rotate → place') compressed into goal-conditioned latents via a temporal abstraction module. A mid-level planner then auto-regressively decodes these into motion primitive latents at finer granularity, each conditioning a low-level action model. We introduce a hierarchical reinforcement signal combining sparse task-completion rewards at the high level with dense motion-consistency rewards at the mid-level, trained jointly via a hierarchical PPO variant. A temporal commitment mechanism prevents low-level thrashing by enforcing latent consistency within subgoal windows.

Experiments: Evaluate on RLBench long-horizon tasks (10+ step sequences), CALVIN benchmark, and real-robot multi-stage assembly. Compare against ThinkAct, SayCan, and hierarchical IL baselines on success rate, replanning frequency, and sample efficiency under distribution shift. Ablate hierarchy depth and commitment window size.

title: LatentPlan Transfer: Cross-Embodiment Visual Plan Latent Adaptation for Zero-Shot Robot Generalization
description: Problem: ThinkAct's visual plan latents are trained and deployed on the same robot embodiment, requiring costly retraining when transferring to robots with different morphologies (e.g., from a 6-DOF arm to a bimanual system or a legged robot). This limits scalability across the robotics ecosystem. Proposed Method: We propose LatentPlan Transfer, which learns a universal visual plan latent space that is embodiment-agnostic by decoupling task-level goal semantics from embodiment-specific kinematics. We train a shared multimodal LLM planner (following ThinkAct's reinforced visual reward framework) across multiple embodiments simultaneously, with an embodiment-conditioned adapter that projects universal plan latents into embodiment-specific action spaces via lightweight cross-attention modules. A contrastive alignment loss enforces that plan latents representing the same task goal cluster together regardless of source embodiment. At test time, only the small adapter is fine-tuned on a few demonstrations from the new robot. Experiments: (1) Zero-shot transfer from simulation embodiments to real robot arms, (2) Cross-morphology transfer between single-arm and bimanual setups on BridgeData V2 and RoboMimic, (3) Ablations on adapter size vs. transfer fidelity, (4) Comparison against full ThinkAct retraining and standard domain adaptation baselines, measuring task success rate and sample efficiency.

title: FailureAct: Learning from Execution Failures via Counterfactual Visual Latent Replanning
description:
Problem: ThinkAct conditions action execution on reasoning plans compressed into visual latents, but when execution fails mid-task, the system lacks a principled mechanism to diagnose why failure occurred and generate corrective replans. Existing VLA approaches treat failures as negative examples to avoid rather than as informative signals for targeted replanning.

Proposed Method: We introduce FailureAct, which extends the ThinkAct dual-system with a failure-aware replanning module. When the action model detects execution failure (via goal-state mismatch rewards), a counterfactual reasoning module queries the multimodal LLM to generate contrastive failure explanations: 'what went wrong and why.' These counterfactual explanations are encoded into corrective visual plan latents that explicitly represent the divergence between intended and observed trajectories. We train this module using a hindsight relabeling strategy that pairs failed trajectories with their counterfactual corrections as reinforcement signal, supplemented by a contrastive latent loss that pushes corrective latents away from failure-inducing ones.

Experiments: (1) RLBench manipulation tasks with deliberate perturbations injected mid-execution; (2) ALFRED household tasks requiring multi-step recovery; (3) Ablations comparing failure-agnostic replanning vs. counterfactual-guided replanning on recovery success rate and number of replanning iterations; (4) Few-shot generalization to novel failure modes unseen during training.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction for VLA Reasoning via Keyframe-Conditioned Latent Planning
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into visual latents but treats temporal structure uniformly, struggling with tasks requiring variable-length sub-goal sequencing (e.g., cooking, assembly) where different sub-tasks demand different temporal granularities. Current VLA frameworks lack mechanisms to dynamically allocate 'thinking budget' across task phases.

Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThink, which extends ThinkAct's dual-system with a hierarchical temporal abstraction layer. A multimodal LLM first decomposes tasks into variable-length sub-goals, predicting keyframe checkpoints at adaptive intervals. Each sub-goal generates an independent visual plan latent via a learned temporal segmentation module trained with a novel 'temporal consistency reward' - reinforcing plans where predicted keyframes align with actual state transitions observed during rollouts. A lightweight temporal attention mechanism dynamically weights which latent to condition the action model on based on current state proximity to predicted keyframes.

Experiments: (1) Long-horizon manipulation benchmarks (RLBench 18-task suite, LIBERO-Long) comparing ThinkAct vs. TemporalThink on task completion and sub-goal accuracy; (2) Variable-complexity tasks requiring dynamic re-planning mid-execution; (3) Ablations on keyframe prediction granularity; (4) Few-shot transfer to novel task compositions; (5) Human evaluation of interpretability of temporal plans. We expect 15-20% improvement on tasks with >5 sequential sub-goals.

title: HierarchicalThink: Compositional Visual Latent Planning with Skill Primitive Discovery for Multi-Task Robot Manipulation
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning into a single visual plan latent, but complex long-horizon tasks benefit from hierarchical decomposition into reusable skill primitives. A flat latent representation struggles to capture compositional structure (e.g., 'open drawer, grasp object, place in container' shares sub-skills across tasks), limiting generalization to novel task combinations.

Proposed Method: We introduce HierarchicalThink, which extends the ThinkAct framework with a two-level visual latent planning hierarchy. At the macro level, a multimodal LLM decomposes instructions into an ordered sequence of skill slots. At the micro level, a learned skill primitive library (codebook of ~64 discrete visual latent codes) represents reusable sub-behaviors discovered via vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) trained jointly with task demonstrations. The macro planner selects skill codes via reinforced planning with both goal-completion and inter-skill transition consistency rewards. The downstream action model is conditioned on the sequentially retrieved skill latents, enabling explicit skill chaining.

Experiments: (1) LIBERO multi-task benchmark measuring compositional generalization to unseen task combinations; (2) RLBench long-horizon tasks comparing planning depth vs. success rate; (3) Ablations on codebook size and hierarchy depth; (4) Zero-shot skill transfer to novel object categories, measuring primitive reuse rate and sample efficiency against ThinkAct and flat-latent baselines.

title: LatentPlan-Transfer: Cross-Embodiment Visual Plan Latent Adaptation for Zero-Shot Robot Transfer
description: Problem: ThinkAct demonstrates that compressing reasoning plans into visual plan latents enables robust action execution, but these latents are learned for specific embodiments (e.g., a particular robot arm). Transferring policies across embodiments with different morphologies, action spaces, and kinematics remains a critical bottleneck in robotics. We hypothesize that visual plan latents, being grounded in goal-state visual representations rather than low-level motor commands, may be embodiment-agnostic and transferable. Proposed Method: We introduce LatentPlan-Transfer, which decouples the visual plan latent space from embodiment-specific action decoders. A shared multimodal LLM generates embodiment-agnostic visual plan latents representing goal completion states and trajectory waypoints. Embodiment-specific adapter modules (lightweight MLPs) then translate these shared latents into robot-specific action sequences. We use cross-embodiment contrastive alignment to ensure that latents encoding the same task goal cluster together regardless of source embodiment. A meta-learning objective enables rapid adapter fine-tuning with <10 demonstrations on new embodiments. Experiments: We evaluate on cross-embodiment transfer between Franka, UR5, and Spot robot platforms using RoboSuite and RLBench benchmarks, measuring zero-shot transfer success rates, few-shot adaptation efficiency, and latent space alignment quality via t-SNE and retrieval metrics across 15 manipulation tasks.

title: HierarchicalThink: Temporally Abstracted Visual Latent Planning with Subgoal Discovery for Long-Horizon Manipulation
description: Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which may lose critical temporal structure for tasks requiring dozens of sequential subgoals (e.g., multi-object assembly, cooking sequences). A flat latent struggles to represent the hierarchical decomposition humans naturally apply to long-horizon tasks. Proposed Method: We introduce HierarchicalThink, which extends the visual latent planning paradigm with automatic subgoal discovery. A multimodal LLM first generates a structured chain-of-thought decomposed into explicit subgoal stages. Each subgoal is independently compressed into a visual plan latent via a learned temporal abstraction module (using vector-quantized codebooks), creating a sequence of discrete latent waypoints. A meta-controller learns when to advance between latent waypoints based on current visual state, while a low-level policy executes within each subgoal's latent context. Training uses hierarchical reinforcement learning: sparse rewards at task completion propagate through subgoal completion bonuses identified via goal-conditioned success detectors. Experiments: (1) CALVIN benchmark with extended 10-task sequences, (2) RLBench multi-stage manipulation tasks, (3) real-robot kitchen assembly requiring 15+ steps. Baselines include ThinkAct, SuSIE, and hierarchical RL methods. Ablations examine codebook size, subgoal granularity, and meta-controller switching strategies. Success metric: task completion rate as horizon length increases.

title: AdaptThink: Online Visual Latent Plan Refinement via Continual Reinforcement in Non-Stationary Environments
description: Problem: ThinkAct and similar dual-system VLA frameworks generate visual latent plans at inference time but treat the environment as stationary — once deployed, the model cannot update its internal planning representations as the environment shifts (e.g., tool wear, dynamic obstacles, distribution-shifted object arrangements). This limits robustness in real-world deployment where conditions change continuously. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptThink, which augments ThinkAct's dual-system architecture with an online continual RL loop that selectively updates the visual plan latent compressor (a lightweight adapter layer) without catastrophic forgetting of the base policy. A surprise-triggered update mechanism monitors discrepancy between predicted and observed visual states; when drift exceeds a threshold, a small batch of recent (state, plan, outcome) tuples triggers a low-rank adapter update via PPO with the same action-aligned visual rewards (goal completion + trajectory consistency). An elastic weight consolidation penalty preserves performance on previously learned tasks. Experiments: (1) Robosuite manipulation tasks with injected mid-episode perturbations (object swaps, lighting changes); (2) ALFRED household tasks across time-varying room configurations; (3) Continual multi-task learning benchmarks measuring forward transfer and backward interference. Baselines include frozen ThinkAct, full fine-tuning, and MAML-style meta-adaptation. Metrics: task success rate under distribution shift, adaptation speed, and catastrophic forgetting score.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction for Long-Horizon VLA Planning via Subgoal-Conditioned Visual Latents
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning into a single visual plan latent, but very long-horizon tasks (e.g., multi-stage kitchen manipulation, multi-room navigation) require structured temporal decomposition where early subgoals must be achieved before later ones become relevant. A flat latent representation cannot capture this sequential dependency structure, limiting performance on tasks requiring 10+ chained subtasks.

Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThink, which extends ThinkAct's dual-system framework with a hierarchical temporal abstraction layer. A multimodal LLM generates an ordered sequence of subgoal reasoning plans rather than a single plan. Each subgoal is compressed into a dedicated visual latent via a learned temporal encoder. A meta-controller monitors execution progress using a learned subgoal completion detector and dynamically switches conditioning latents when a subgoal is achieved, enabling adaptive re-planning upon failure. Subgoal transitions are trained with a curriculum of progressively longer task horizons using group relative policy optimization (GRPO), rewarding both individual subgoal completion and full-task success.

Experiments: (1) ALFRED long-horizon household tasks comparing flat vs. hierarchical latents; (2) RLBench multi-stage manipulation benchmarks (10+ step sequences); (3) Ablations on subgoal granularity and transition detection accuracy; (4) Robustness evaluation under mid-task perturbations measuring self-correction via latent switching. Baseline comparisons against ThinkAct, SayCan, and RT-2.

title: HierarchPlan: Compositional Visual Latent Planning via Skill-Level Abstraction for Multi-Task Robot Generalization
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, but complex long-horizon tasks often require hierarchical decomposition—high-level task sequencing and low-level skill parameterization—which a flat latent representation may fail to capture. A unified latent conflates 'what subtasks to do' with 'how to execute each subtask,' limiting compositional generalization to novel task combinations.

Proposed Method: We introduce HierarchPlan, a two-level visual latent planning framework. A high-level planner (multimodal LLM) decomposes task instructions into an ordered sequence of skill tokens, each compressed into a skill-level latent via a VQ-VAE codebook trained on skill demonstrations. A low-level controller receives each skill latent as a conditioning signal and produces motor actions. Skill latents are learned jointly through a compositional reinforcement objective: task-completion rewards propagated hierarchically, plus a skill-boundary detection auxiliary loss encouraging clean subtask transitions. At inference, novel tasks are addressed by recombining learned skill latents without retraining.

Experiments: (1) CALVIN multi-task benchmark measuring compositional generalization to unseen task sequences; (2) RLBench long-horizon manipulation tasks; (3) Few-shot adaptation with 5/10/20 demonstrations per novel task; (4) Ablations comparing flat vs. hierarchical latents, codebook sizes, and reward propagation schemes.

title: LatentPlan-Transfer: Cross-Embodiment Visual Plan Latent Adaptation for Zero-Shot Robot Skill Transfer
description: Problem: ThinkAct demonstrates that compressing reasoning into visual plan latents enables robust action execution, but these latents are trained and evaluated within a single embodiment. A critical open question is whether visual plan latents encode embodiment-agnostic task semantics (what to do) separable from embodiment-specific motor execution (how to do it), enabling zero-shot transfer across robots with different morphologies and action spaces. Method: We propose LatentPlan-Transfer, which learns a shared visual plan latent space across multiple source embodiments (e.g., Franka arm, UR5, mobile manipulator) by training embodiment-invariant plan encoders with contrastive alignment losses that encourage latents representing the same task goal to cluster regardless of robot morphology. A lightweight embodiment-conditioned adapter then maps shared latents to target-embodiment action sequences. During inference on a novel robot, only the adapter is fine-tuned with minimal demonstrations while the plan latent space remains frozen. Experiments: We evaluate on Cross-Embodiment Manipulation Benchmark (CEMB) and RoboAgent across 4 robot platforms, measuring zero-shot task success rate, sample efficiency of adapter fine-tuning (1/5/10-shot), and latent space alignment via mutual information metrics. Ablations compare full fine-tuning vs. adapter-only vs. our shared latent approach, testing whether semantic structure is genuinely preserved across embodiments.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction for Long-Horizon VLA Planning via Keyframe-Conditioned Latent Reasoning
description: Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which loses temporal structure critical for long-horizon tasks requiring sequential sub-goal completion across dozens of steps. A flat latent representation conflates near-term and far-future intentions, limiting adaptive replanning when intermediate sub-goals fail. Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThink, extending the dual-system framework with hierarchical temporal abstractions. Rather than a single visual plan latent, we generate a sequence of keyframe latents at multiple timescales: coarse goal keyframes (task completion), mid-level milestone keyframes (sub-task transitions), and fine-grained execution keyframes (immediate actions). A temporal attention mechanism in the action model selectively attends to the appropriate abstraction level given current progress. We train the hierarchy using a multi-level reinforcement reward: sparse goal-completion rewards shape coarse latents, dense trajectory-consistency rewards shape fine latents, and a novel 'milestone detection' reward (using vision-language grounding to identify sub-task boundaries) shapes mid-level latents. Experiments: We evaluate on CALVIN benchmark extended to 10-step sequences, Meta-World multi-stage manipulation, and a new household task-completion benchmark requiring 20+ step planning. We compare against ThinkAct, SuSIE, and GR-1, measuring task completion rate, replanning success after perturbations, and temporal coherence of generated keyframes.

title: PlanDiff: Diffusion-Based Visual Plan Latent Generation for Stochastic Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single deterministic visual plan latent, which struggles to represent the inherent multimodality of long-horizon tasks where multiple valid execution paths exist. In stochastic environments with object clutter, occlusions, or ambiguous instructions, a unimodal latent fails to capture plan uncertainty, leading to brittle execution when the initial plan becomes infeasible mid-task.

Proposed Method: We introduce PlanDiff, which replaces ThinkAct's deterministic plan latent encoder with a conditional diffusion model that generates a distribution over visual plan latents. Given multimodal LLM reasoning outputs as conditioning, PlanDiff samples diverse candidate plan latents via reverse diffusion, ranks them using a learned feasibility critic trained on trajectory outcomes, and passes the highest-ranked latent to the action model. During execution, if an anomaly detector identifies plan deviation, PlanDiff resamples a new latent conditioned on the current observation, enabling online replanning without full LLM re-inference.

Experiments: (1) CALVIN benchmark with added stochastic perturbations (object displacement mid-task); (2) RLBench multi-step tasks comparing success rate vs. ThinkAct baseline; (3) Ablations on number of diffusion samples and replanning frequency; (4) Visualization of sampled plan latent diversity via t-SNE to confirm multimodal coverage. We expect 15-20% improvement in task completion under perturbation.

title: AdaptThink: Online Continual Reinforcement of Visual Latent Plans for Non-Stationary Embodied Environments
description:
Problem: ThinkAct and similar VLA frameworks assume relatively stationary target environments during deployment. Real-world robotic settings exhibit non-stationarity — objects shift, lighting changes, new task variations emerge — causing pre-trained visual plan latents to drift from current environment dynamics, degrading performance over time without retraining.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptThink, an online continual learning extension of the dual-system VLA paradigm. During deployment, the agent maintains a small episodic memory buffer of recent trajectory segments with associated reward signals. A lightweight meta-gradient update rule selectively refreshes only the visual plan latent encoder and conditioning adapter using contrastive plan consistency loss, preserving the frozen reasoning LLM backbone to avoid catastrophic forgetting. We further introduce an uncertainty-aware gating mechanism: when predicted plan latent confidence falls below a threshold (measured via ensemble disagreement), the system triggers active re-planning rather than executing stale plans.

Experiments: (1) FurnitureBench with progressive layout randomization across episodes; (2) CALVIN benchmark with incremental task-type introduction; (3) a custom non-stationary variant of MetaWorld with object property shifts. We compare against ThinkAct baseline, EWC regularization, and experience replay baselines, measuring adaptation speed, forward transfer, and catastrophic forgetting metrics across environment shifts.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction in Visual Latent Planning for Multi-Stage Manipulation Tasks
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which may lose critical temporal structure for tasks requiring distinct sequential phases (e.g., grasp→transport→assemble→verify). A flat latent representation struggles to condition action execution across qualitatively different sub-task stages with varying dynamics and success criteria.

Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThink, which extends ThinkAct's visual latent planning with a hierarchical temporal abstraction. Instead of one global plan latent, a multimodal LLM generates temporally segmented reasoning chains that are encoded into a sequence of sub-goal latents via a learned temporal segmentation module. A meta-controller selects the active sub-goal latent based on detected phase transitions (using a lightweight progress estimator), feeding stage-appropriate conditioning to the action model. We introduce a temporal consistency reward that penalizes out-of-order sub-goal activation and a phase completion reward derived from visual goal matching at each stage boundary. Training uses PPO with the combined reward signal.

Experiments: (1) RLBench multi-stage manipulation (10+ step tasks), (2) ALFRED household task benchmark, (3) real-robot assembly tasks. Ablations compare single-latent vs. hierarchical latents, fixed vs. adaptive phase transitions, and varying numbers of sub-goal levels. Metrics include task completion rate, replanning frequency, and sub-task ordering accuracy.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction for Long-Horizon VLA Planning via Keyframe-Anchored Latent Imagination
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which loses temporal structure critical for very long-horizon tasks (50+ steps) where intermediate subgoals must be reached sequentially. A flat latent representation forces the action model to implicitly recover temporal ordering, limiting scalability to extended manipulation sequences.

Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThink, which extends the dual-system framework by replacing the single visual plan latent with a sequence of keyframe-anchored temporal latents. A multimodal LLM first predicts a structured plan as an ordered set of keyframe descriptions (subgoal states). A diffusion-based keyframe imagination module generates visual embeddings for each predicted subgoal, conditioned on the current observation. These temporally ordered latents are consumed by a recurrent action model that transitions between subgoal-conditioned policies, with a learned progress estimator detecting subgoal completion to advance the latent sequence. Reinforcement learning rewards incorporate subgoal-reaching bonuses alongside trajectory consistency, training the full pipeline end-to-end.

Experiments: (1) CALVIN benchmark extended to 6-task chains, (2) RLBench long-horizon tasks (20+ step sequences), (3) LIBERO task suite measuring subgoal decomposition accuracy, (4) ablations comparing flat vs. temporal latents, (5) few-shot generalization to novel task orderings. We expect 15-25% improvement over ThinkAct on tasks exceeding 30 steps.

title: LatentPlan Transfer: Cross-Embodiment Visual Plan Compression for Zero-Shot Robot Adaptation
description: Problem: ThinkAct demonstrates that compressing reasoning plans into visual plan latents enables effective robot manipulation, but these latents are learned per-embodiment. When deploying to new robot morphologies (e.g., from a 7-DOF arm to a bimanual system or mobile manipulator), the visual plan latents must be retrained from scratch, limiting scalability across the diverse robot ecosystem. Proposed Method: We propose LatentPlan Transfer, a framework that learns embodiment-agnostic visual plan latents by disentangling task-level intent from embodiment-specific motor constraints. We train a shared visual plan encoder across multiple robot embodiments using a contrastive alignment objective that enforces semantic similarity between plans achieving equivalent task outcomes despite different kinematic structures. A lightweight embodiment adapter module then translates shared latents into embodiment-specific action conditions using only a small number of demonstration rollouts (5-10). We additionally introduce an embodiment-invariant reward signal based on object-state transitions rather than trajectory shape to guide reinforcement. Experiments: We evaluate on cross-embodiment transfer across three robot platforms (Franka, UR5, bimanual setup) in RoboSuite and real-world tasks, measuring zero-shot and few-shot success rates, plan latent alignment quality via t-SNE clustering, and self-correction under morphology-induced perturbations. Baselines include ThinkAct per-embodiment training, RT-2 fine-tuning, and embodiment-agnostic world models.

title: AdaptThink: Online Visual Latent Plan Refinement via Continual Reinforcement Learning in Non-Stationary Environments
description: Problem: ThinkAct generates visual plan latents at inference time but treats the environment as stationary — once deployed, the model cannot update its internal planning representations as the environment drifts (e.g., objects rearranged, lighting changes, novel obstacles). This limits long-term deployment robustness without costly retraining. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptThink, which extends ThinkAct's dual-system framework with a continual online RL loop that refines the visual plan latent encoder during deployment. Specifically, we maintain a small episodic replay buffer of recent trajectory-reward pairs and apply lightweight LoRA updates to the plan latent compression module using a combination of goal-completion rewards and temporal consistency penalties. To prevent catastrophic forgetting, we employ Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) anchored to the pretrained ThinkAct weights. A change-detection module monitors distribution shift in incoming visual observations and triggers adaptation selectively, controlling compute overhead. Planned Experiments: (1) Tabletop manipulation with programmatic environment perturbations (object clutter added mid-deployment) in RLBench; (2) Long-horizon household navigation in AI2-THOR with dynamic furniture rearrangement; (3) Ablations comparing EWC vs. rehearsal vs. no-regularization under increasing perturbation severity; (4) Sample efficiency analysis measuring performance recovery steps after distributional shift versus static ThinkAct baseline.

title: TemporalPlan: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction for VLA Reasoning via Skill-Conditioned Latent Planning
description: Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which may lose critical temporal structure for long-horizon tasks requiring sequenced sub-goals. Current VLA frameworks lack explicit mechanisms for decomposing tasks into reusable temporal skill primitives, limiting generalization to novel task orderings or mid-task interruptions. Method: We propose TemporalPlan, which extends the dual-system VLA paradigm with hierarchical temporal abstraction. A multimodal LLM first decomposes task instructions into an ordered sequence of skill tokens, each grounded in predicted visual keyframe states. These skill tokens are learned as a discrete latent codebook via VQ-VAE trained jointly with reinforcement learning rewards measuring sub-goal completion. A temporal attention mechanism in the downstream action model conditions execution on the current skill token and predicted future keyframe, enabling the agent to dynamically advance or re-attempt skills based on execution feedback. Planned Experiments: (1) Long-horizon manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO-Long, RLBench) measuring task success across 10+ step sequences; (2) Mid-task recovery evaluation where tasks are artificially interrupted, testing self-correction without replanning from scratch; (3) Cross-task skill transfer: measuring zero-shot reuse of learned skill primitives on unseen task compositions; (4) Ablations comparing single-latent (ThinkAct-style) versus hierarchical skill decomposition.

title: TemporalThink: Causal Temporal Reasoning for Video-Based VLA Models via Counterfactual Visual Plan Latents
description:
Problem: ThinkAct generates visual plan latents conditioned on current observations, but lacks explicit causal temporal reasoning — understanding how past actions causally influenced current states and how hypothetical future actions would alter outcomes. This limits performance on tasks requiring counterfactual reasoning (e.g., 'if I had placed the cup differently, would stacking succeed?') and recovery from compounding errors in long-horizon manipulation.

Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThink, which augments the ThinkAct dual-system framework with a counterfactual visual plan latent module. A multimodal LLM is trained to generate not only forward plans but also counterfactual rollouts — imagined trajectories under alternative past actions — using a contrastive temporal reward that penalizes latent representations indistinguishable between successful and failed counterfactual branches. These causal plan latents are encoded via a temporal causal graph that explicitly models state-action dependencies across time, conditioning the downstream action model on both the intended future and the causal history.

Experiments: We evaluate on (1) RLBench long-horizon manipulation tasks with induced mid-task perturbations, (2) CALVIN benchmark for multi-stage instruction following, and (3) a novel 'causal recovery' benchmark where agents must diagnose and correct specific past action errors. We compare against ThinkAct, RT-2, and SayCan baselines on success rate, recovery rate, and step efficiency.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction for Long-Horizon VLA Planning via Keyframe-Conditioned Latent Compression
description: Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which struggles to represent temporally extended tasks requiring distinct sub-goal checkpoints (e.g., 10+ step household manipulation). A flat latent bottleneck loses temporal structure critical for adaptive re-planning mid-task. Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThink, which decomposes visual plan latents into a sequence of keyframe-aligned sub-goal latents using a hierarchical variational encoder. A high-level planner (multimodal LLM) generates structured reasoning chains decomposed into K sub-goals; each sub-goal is encoded into a compact latent via contrastive keyframe grounding against predicted future observations. A temporal gating mechanism dynamically switches between sub-goal latents conditioned on environment feedback, enabling online re-planning when execution deviates from predictions. Training combines ThinkAct-style reinforced visual rewards with a temporal consistency loss penalizing sub-goal ordering violations. Experiments: (1) ALFRED and BEHAVIOR-1K long-horizon household tasks measuring sub-goal completion rate and replanning frequency; (2) Meta-World multi-stage manipulation with deliberate mid-task perturbations testing recovery; (3) Ablations comparing flat vs. hierarchical latent compression at varying task horizons (5/10/20 steps); (4) Few-shot generalization to novel task compositions unseen during training.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction in Visual Latent Planning for Multi-Stage Manipulation Tasks
description: Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which struggles when tasks require dynamically switching between qualitatively different sub-skills (e.g., grasping → assembling → quality-checking) across long horizons. A flat latent fails to capture the hierarchical temporal structure inherent in multi-stage tasks. Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThink, extending ThinkAct's dual-system framework with a hierarchical visual latent planning mechanism. A multimodal LLM generates a structured plan decomposed into ordered sub-goal stages. Each stage is encoded into a distinct temporal latent vector via a stage-conditioned VQ-VAE, producing a latent sequence rather than a single vector. A temporal attention mechanism over this latent sequence dynamically selects the active stage latent to condition the low-level action model based on current visual observations. We introduce a hierarchical reinforcement signal combining: (1) sub-goal completion rewards at stage boundaries detected via vision-language grounding, (2) inter-stage transition smoothness penalties, and (3) overall task completion rewards. Experiments: We evaluate on FurnitureBench (multi-stage assembly), CLIPort long-horizon tasks, and a new 10-stage kitchen manipulation benchmark. We compare against ThinkAct, SuSIE, and hierarchical RL baselines on success rate, stage completion rate, and recovery from mid-task perturbations.

title: HierarchicalThink: Temporally Abstracted Visual Latent Planning with Subgoal Discovery for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
description: Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning into a single visual plan latent, which struggles when tasks require hundreds of steps with compositional structure (e.g., multi-stage assembly, cooking). A flat latent cannot efficiently represent hierarchical dependencies between distant subgoals. Proposed Method: We introduce HierarchicalThink, which extends ThinkAct's dual-system framework with an automatic subgoal discovery mechanism. A multimodal LLM first segments the task into temporally abstract subgoals via chain-of-thought reasoning, then generates a sequence of visual plan latents—one per subgoal—rather than a single global latent. We train a subgoal-conditioned options network using hierarchical reinforcement learning, where high-level policies select which latent to activate and low-level policies execute primitive actions conditioned on the active subgoal latent. Subgoal boundaries are discovered using a learned temporal contrast objective that maximizes mutual information between visual observations and subgoal transitions. A subgoal completion critic provides intermediate dense rewards, alleviating sparse reward problems in long-horizon settings. Experiments: We evaluate on CALVIN long-horizon benchmarks (1000+ step tasks), RLBench multi-stage manipulation, and a new 20-stage tabletop assembly suite we introduce. We compare against ThinkAct, GROOT, and SuSIE on task completion rate, subgoal accuracy, and adaptation efficiency under novel instruction variations.

title: HierarchicalThink: Multi-Granularity Visual Latent Planning with Temporal Abstraction for Long-Horizon Manipulation
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which loses temporal structure for tasks requiring dozens of sequential sub-goals. A flat latent cannot distinguish between immediate next-step intentions and distant goal states, limiting performance on extended manipulation sequences (e.g., multi-object assembly, cooking tasks).

Proposed Method: We introduce HierarchicalThink, which extends ThinkAct's dual-system framework with a three-level temporal abstraction hierarchy. A multimodal LLM generates plans decomposed into (1) macro-goals (task completion), (2) meso-steps (sub-goal milestones), and (3) micro-actions (immediate primitives). Each level is compressed into a separate visual plan latent via a hierarchical VQ-VAE. A temporal gating mechanism dynamically switches conditioning from macro to micro latents based on estimated sub-goal completion confidence, predicted via an auxiliary progress estimator trained with contrastive self-supervised rewards. The action model receives multi-resolution latent conditioning, enabling adaptive re-planning at different timescales without full replanning overhead.

Experiments: We evaluate on LIBERO-Long, RLBench multi-stage tasks, and a new 30-step assembly benchmark we introduce. Ablations compare single vs. hierarchical latents, fixed vs. dynamic gating, and measure replanning frequency vs. task success rate. We demonstrate superior performance on tasks requiring 20+ sequential sub-goals compared to ThinkAct and flat-latent baselines.

title: AdaptThink: Online Visual Latent Plan Adaptation via Failure-Driven Contrastive Refinement
description: Problem: ThinkAct generates visual plan latents at inference time but treats them as fixed during execution. When unexpected perturbations occur mid-task (object displacement, grasp failure, dynamic obstacles), the stale latent plan leads to compounding errors without recovery. Existing self-correction relies on replanning from scratch, which is computationally expensive and disrupts temporal continuity. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptThink, which augments ThinkAct with an online latent plan adaptation module. A lightweight anomaly detector monitors execution trajectory deviation using optical flow and proprioceptive residuals. Upon detecting failure, rather than full replanning, we perform contrastive latent refinement: the current visual plan latent is updated via gradient steps that maximize similarity to successful sub-goal embeddings from a dynamically maintained episodic memory bank while minimizing similarity to failure-state embeddings. This yields targeted latent corrections without re-invoking the full multimodal LLM. The adapted latent then re-conditions the downstream action model for corrective execution. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) MetaWorld with mid-episode perturbations, (2) FurnitureBench long-horizon assembly with randomized disturbances, and (3) a real-robot pick-and-place task with adversarial object displacements. Metrics include recovery rate, replanning latency, and task completion under varying perturbation frequencies, compared against ThinkAct, replanning baselines, and residual policy methods.

title: AdaptThink: Online Continual Adaptation of Visual Latent Plans via Failure-Driven Contrastive Reinforcement
description: Problem: ThinkAct demonstrates strong few-shot adaptation but assumes a fixed environment distribution at deployment. Real-world robots encounter non-stationary environments where object configurations, lighting, and task semantics shift over time, causing visual plan latents to become stale and action execution to degrade without costly retraining. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptThink, an online continual learning extension of the ThinkAct framework. When the action model detects execution failures (via a lightweight outcome classifier monitoring gripper force, task completion signals, or visual mismatch), AdaptThink triggers a contrastive latent refinement step: the multimodal LLM generates corrective reasoning traces comparing the failed trajectory against successful demonstrations retrieved from a compact episodic memory buffer. A contrastive reinforcement objective updates only the visual plan latent encoder using triplets (current context, failure trajectory, success trajectory), preserving the frozen action model while adapting the plan representation to the new distribution. A synaptic consolidation regularizer prevents catastrophic forgetting of prior tasks. Experiments: We evaluate on RLBench with dynamically injected distribution shifts (novel objects, rearranged clutter, lighting changes), LIBERO continual manipulation suites, and a real Franka Panda setup. Metrics include forward transfer, backward transfer, adaptation speed (episodes to recovery), and comparison against LoRA fine-tuning and experience replay baselines.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction for Long-Horizon VLA Planning via Subgoal-Conditioned Visual Latents
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which may be insufficient for very long-horizon tasks requiring dozens of sequential subgoals with conditional branching (e.g., household rearrangement, multi-stage assembly). A flat latent representation cannot adequately capture the temporal dependency structure between intermediate milestones.

Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThink, which extends ThinkAct's dual-system framework with a hierarchical latent planning stack. A high-level multimodal LLM generates an ordered sequence of subgoal descriptions; a temporal abstraction module encodes these into a structured chain of visual plan latents using a learned subgoal-conditioned diffusion process. At inference time, an online subgoal completion detector—trained with contrastive rewards between predicted and achieved visual states—triggers progression to the next latent in the chain, enabling dynamic replanning when subgoals fail. A secondary RL objective penalizes unnecessary subgoal repetition and rewards efficient temporal progression.

Experiments: (1) ALFRED benchmark for multi-step household tasks; (2) RLBench long-horizon manipulation sequences (10+ stage tasks); (3) Ablations comparing flat vs. hierarchical latents on task completion rate and replanning frequency; (4) Few-shot generalization to novel task orderings; (5) Human evaluation of interpretability of generated subgoal sequences versus baseline ThinkAct.

title: HierarchicalCorrAct: Temporal Credit Assignment for Multi-Step Self-Correction in Vision-Language-Action Models via Contrastive Latent Replay
description: Problem: ThinkAct demonstrates self-correction behavior, but the reinforcement signal used to train visual latent planning treats each correction episode independently, ignoring temporal credit assignment across multi-step correction chains. When an agent makes an error at step t and corrects it at step t+k, the reward signal poorly attributes which intermediate reasoning steps enabled recovery, limiting learning efficiency for long-horizon self-correction. Proposed Method: We introduce HierarchicalCorrAct, which extends the visual latent planning framework with a contrastive latent replay mechanism. We maintain a correction memory buffer storing (failed_latent, successful_correction_latent, outcome_reward) tuples. A hierarchical credit assignment module learns to contrast failed vs. successful reasoning latents at each correction step using a temporally-discounted contrastive objective, explicitly identifying which latent subspace transitions correlate with recovery. These contrastive gradients augment the base reinforcement signal during VLA training. Additionally, we introduce a correction-chain reward that provides dense intermediate rewards for partial recovery trajectories rather than sparse terminal rewards. Experiments: (1) Long-horizon manipulation benchmarks (RLBench, CALVIN) with deliberately injected perturbations requiring 3-5 correction steps; (2) Few-shot adaptation to novel disturbances; (3) Ablations on credit assignment depth and buffer composition; (4) Comparison against ThinkAct baseline on correction success rate and recovery efficiency metrics.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction in Visual Latent Planning for Multi-Stage Manipulation
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which struggles to capture the temporal structure of long-horizon tasks requiring sequential sub-goal achievement (e.g., 'open drawer, grasp object, place in container, close drawer'). A flat latent representation conflates distinct temporal phases, limiting fine-grained action conditioning across task stages.

Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThink, which extends the visual latent planning paradigm with hierarchical temporal abstraction. Rather than a single plan latent, we train the multimodal LLM to generate temporally segmented reasoning plans that are compressed into an ordered sequence of sub-goal latents via a learned temporal chunking mechanism. A lightweight transformer-based temporal scheduler dynamically selects the active sub-goal latent conditioned on current visual observations and execution progress. Sub-goal transitions are learned via a progress-aware reward that combines ThinkAct's goal-completion signal with a novel sub-goal boundary detection reward derived from contrastive temporal embedding distances.

Experiments: (1) CALVIN multi-stage manipulation benchmark comparing against ThinkAct and hierarchical RL baselines on 5-task chains; (2) RLBench multi-step tasks measuring sub-goal transition accuracy and recovery from mid-task failures; (3) Ablation of temporal chunking granularity and scheduler architectures; (4) Few-shot generalization to novel task orderings unseen during training.

title: HierarchicalThink: Temporal Abstraction in Visual Latent Planning via Multi-Scale Reasoning Compression
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, treating all planning horizons uniformly. This fails to capture the inherently hierarchical nature of long-horizon tasks where abstract sub-goals (e.g., 'open cabinet') must coordinate multiple primitive actions over varying timescales. A flat latent bottleneck loses temporal structure critical for tasks requiring dynamic re-planning mid-execution.

Method: We propose HierarchicalThink, extending the visual latent planning paradigm with multi-scale temporal abstraction. A multimodal LLM generates reasoning plans at three granularities: task-level goals, sub-goal sequences, and primitive action scripts. These are compressed into a hierarchy of visual plan latents using a temporal pyramid encoder, where coarser latents condition finer ones via cross-attention gating. Reinforcement learning rewards operate at each hierarchy level—task completion, sub-goal achievement, and trajectory smoothness—enabling credit assignment across timescales. A learned temporal scheduler dynamically selects which latent level to reactivate upon detecting execution failures via visual discrepancy detection.

Experiments: We evaluate on CALVIN long-horizon manipulation benchmarks (5+ chained tasks), RLBench multi-stage manipulation, and a new household rearrangement suite requiring 10+ step planning. Ablations compare flat vs. hierarchical latents, fixed vs. dynamic scheduling, and single vs. multi-level RL rewards. We measure task success rate, replanning frequency, and adaptation speed under mid-task perturbations.

title: HierarchicalThink: Multi-Granularity Visual Latent Planning with Temporal Abstraction for Long-Horizon Manipulation
description:
Problem: ThinkAct generates reasoning plans at a single temporal granularity, which struggles with long-horizon tasks requiring both strategic (task-level) and tactical (subtask-level) reasoning simultaneously. A robot assembling furniture, for instance, needs to reason about both the overall assembly sequence and precise manipulation primitives within each step.

Proposed Method: We introduce HierarchicalThink, a three-level planning architecture that extends ThinkAct's visual latent planning with explicit temporal abstraction. A high-level planner generates goal-conditioned subgoal sequences as coarse visual latents (semantic keyframes), a mid-level planner decomposes each subgoal into motion primitives as fine-grained latents, and a low-level controller executes actions. Each level is trained with level-specific reinforcement rewards: subgoal completion rates for the high-level, primitive success rates for the mid-level, and trajectory smoothness for the low-level. A hierarchical consistency reward aligns representations across levels, encouraging coherent multi-granularity planning.

Experiments: (1) CALVIN benchmark with extended 6-step task chains, (2) FurnitureBench assembly tasks requiring 20+ step sequences, (3) RLBench multi-stage manipulation tasks. We measure task completion rate, planning efficiency, and self-correction frequency at each abstraction level. Ablations examine the contribution of each planning granularity and cross-level consistency rewards versus single-level baselines.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction in Visual Latent Planning for Long-Horizon Manipulation via Option-Conditioned Reinforcement
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, but long-horizon tasks requiring dozens of subtasks suffer from information bottlenecks when all temporal structure is collapsed into one representation. Current approaches lack explicit temporal abstraction, forcing the action model to infer task progression implicitly.

Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThink, which extends ThinkAct's dual-system framework with a hierarchical latent planning structure inspired by options theory. Rather than one visual plan latent, the multimodal LLM generates a sequence of K subgoal latents at adaptive temporal granularities, learned via a multi-level reinforcement objective combining: (1) subgoal completion rewards, (2) inter-subgoal temporal consistency penalties, and (3) a duration predictor that learns when to commit to the next subgoal. A lightweight temporal attention mechanism in the downstream action model selects which latent to condition on based on current state, enabling dynamic subgoal switching and mid-execution self-correction.

Experiments: We evaluate on CALVIN benchmark (multi-stage manipulation), RLBench long-horizon tasks (10+ step sequences), and a new household rearrangement benchmark requiring 20+ primitive actions. Ablations compare single vs. hierarchical latents, fixed vs. adaptive temporal granularity, and measure self-correction frequency when subtask failures occur. Baselines include ThinkAct, SuSIE, and hierarchical diffusion planners.

title: LatentPlan Transfer: Cross-Embodiment Visual Plan Representations for Zero-Shot Robot Adaptation
description: Problem: ThinkAct demonstrates compelling embodied reasoning within a single robot morphology, but real-world deployment requires adapting learned visual plan latents across fundamentally different embodiments (e.g., from a 7-DOF arm to a mobile manipulator or humanoid). The visual plan latent space learned in ThinkAct may be embodiment-specific, limiting transferability. Method: We propose LatentPlan Transfer, which disentangles the visual plan latent into two components: a morphology-agnostic task semantics representation encoding goal states and trajectory intent, and a morphology-specific execution code. We train a contrastive alignment objective that encourages equivalent tasks across different robot embodiments to share identical semantic latents while diverging in execution codes. A lightweight adapter module then translates shared semantic latents into embodiment-specific action conditioning for each target robot. The semantic latent space is regularized via cross-embodiment consistency rewards derived from ThinkAct's reinforcement framework. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) RoboMimic and MetaWorld with paired multi-embodiment task suites, (2) zero-shot transfer from simulation-trained agents to real robot hardware, and (3) few-shot adaptation efficiency compared to full ThinkAct fine-tuning. We measure task success rate, latent alignment quality via mutual information metrics, and adaptation sample efficiency across 5 embodiment pairs.

title: HierPlan: Hierarchical Visual Latent Planning with Uncertainty-Aware Subgoal Decomposition for Long-Horizon Manipulation
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which may lose critical intermediate state information for very long-horizon tasks (10+ steps) where subgoal dependencies are complex. A flat latent representation struggles to capture hierarchical task structure, leading to compounding errors over extended horizons.

Proposed Method: We propose HierPlan, which extends visual latent planning into a hierarchical structure. A high-level multimodal LLM decomposes tasks into a sequence of temporally-grounded subgoal latents, each representing an intermediate visual state milestone. A learned uncertainty estimator (using ensemble disagreement over predicted subgoal latents) flags when subgoal confidence is low, triggering re-planning via the LLM. A mid-level subgoal executor conditions on individual subgoal latents sequentially, while a low-level action primitive policy handles fine-grained execution. Subgoal latents are trained with both visual reward alignment and subgoal reachability signals derived from offline trajectory data.

Experiments: (1) CALVIN benchmark extending to 5-10 task chains; (2) RLBench long-horizon multi-stage tasks; (3) Ablations on flat vs. hierarchical latents, uncertainty-triggered replanning frequency, and subgoal granularity; (4) Robustness evaluation under mid-task perturbations comparing self-correction rates against ThinkAct baseline; (5) Few-shot generalization to novel task sequences.

title: LatentDebate: Improving Visual Plan Latents via Multi-Agent Adversarial Reasoning in Embodied AI
description: Problem: ThinkAct compresses a single reasoning chain into a visual plan latent, but a single planner may generate overconfident or suboptimal plans in ambiguous environments, lacking diversity and robustness in plan representations. Proposed Method: We introduce LatentDebate, a multi-agent adversarial reasoning framework where two specialized multimodal LLMs—a 'proposer' and a 'critic'—engage in structured debate rounds before committing to a visual plan latent. The proposer generates candidate embodied reasoning plans; the critic identifies failure modes, inconsistencies, or risky subgoals using environment feedback; the proposer revises accordingly. After N debate rounds, the final plan latent is constructed as a weighted ensemble of proposal and critique embeddings, gated by a learned confidence module trained with RL rewards identical to ThinkAct (goal completion + trajectory consistency). The gated latent then conditions a downstream action model. The debate loop is terminated early via a convergence criterion based on latent cosine similarity between rounds. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) ALFRED long-horizon household tasks, (2) RLBench manipulation with perturbations, and (3) a new adversarial variant of MetaWorld where object positions shift mid-episode. Metrics include task success rate, self-correction frequency, and plan latent diversity scores. We compare against ThinkAct, chain-of-thought baselines, and ensemble planning methods.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction for Long-Horizon VLA Reasoning via Multi-Scale Latent Planning
description: Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, but long-horizon tasks with distinct task phases (e.g., 'set table, cook meal, serve') require reasoning at multiple temporal scales simultaneously. A flat latent representation conflates coarse strategic goals with fine-grained tactical steps, limiting adaptation when mid-task conditions change unexpectedly. Method: We propose TemporalThink, which extends the dual-system VLA framework with a hierarchical multi-scale latent planner. A multimodal LLM generates plans at three abstraction levels—strategic (goal), tactical (subtask), and reactive (step)—each compressed into separate latent vectors via scale-specific VQ-VAE encoders. A temporal gating mechanism dynamically selects which latent scale to condition the action model on based on observed task progress and uncertainty estimates from the action model's internal states. Reinforcement rewards are defined per scale: completion reward for strategic latents, subtask transition accuracy for tactical, and trajectory smoothness for reactive. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) ALFRED benchmark for household long-horizon tasks, (2) RLBench multi-stage manipulation suites, and (3) a newly constructed 'interrupted task recovery' benchmark where environmental perturbations force mid-execution replanning. We compare against ThinkAct, SayCan, and RT-2 baselines, measuring task completion rate, replanning efficiency, and cross-task generalization.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction in Visual Latent Planning for Multi-Stage Manipulation Tasks
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which struggles to capture the hierarchical temporal structure of long-horizon tasks requiring distinct sequential sub-goals (e.g., open drawer → grasp object → place in container). A flat latent representation conflates near-term and long-term intentions, limiting adaptation when intermediate sub-goals fail or environmental conditions change mid-execution.

Method: We propose TemporalThink, which extends the visual latent planning framework with a hierarchical temporal abstraction mechanism. Instead of a single plan latent, we learn a sequence of sub-goal latents at multiple timescales using a temporal hierarchy encoder trained with contrastive sub-goal consistency losses. Each sub-goal latent is generated autoregressively conditioned on task completion signals from the previous stage, detected via lightweight vision-based success classifiers. A gating mechanism dynamically selects which temporal level conditions the low-level action model, enabling graceful recovery when sub-goals are reordered or interrupted.

Experiments: (1) RLBench multi-stage tasks (10+ step horizons) comparing flat vs. hierarchical latents on success rate and recovery rate after perturbation; (2) LIBERO benchmark for few-shot transfer across task variants; (3) Real-robot tabletop manipulation with deliberate mid-task disruptions measuring self-correction frequency; (4) Ablations on hierarchy depth, sub-goal detection accuracy, and latent dimensionality.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction in Visual Latent Planning for Multi-Stage Manipulation Tasks
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, which loses temporal structure critical for long-horizon tasks with distinct sequential phases (e.g., open drawer → grasp object → place in container). A flat latent representation forces the action model to infer temporal ordering implicitly, limiting performance on tasks requiring precise phase transitions.

Proposed Method: TemporalThink introduces a hierarchical temporal decomposition into the visual latent planning framework. Rather than a single plan latent, we generate a sequence of K sub-goal latents via a learned temporal segmentation module that divides the multimodal LLM's reasoning plan into ordered phase representations. Each sub-goal latent conditions the action model only during its corresponding execution window, determined by a learned phase-transition detector that monitors visual state embeddings. We train the segmentation module using a curriculum of reinforcement signals: intra-phase trajectory consistency rewards and inter-phase milestone completion rewards, encouraging clean temporal boundaries.

Experiments: (1) Long-horizon manipulation benchmarks (RLBench 18-task suite, CALVIN) comparing against ThinkAct and flat-latent baselines on task completion rate and phase-transition accuracy. (2) Ablations on number of sub-goals K and transition detection thresholds. (3) Few-shot generalization to novel task sequences not seen during training. (4) Visualization of learned temporal segmentation against human-annotated phase boundaries.

title: LatentPlan-Transfer: Cross-Embodiment Visual Plan Latent Adaptation for Zero-Shot Robot Skill Transfer
description:
Problem: While ThinkAct demonstrates that visual plan latents can condition action execution, these latents are learned for specific embodiments (e.g., a particular robot morphology). When transferring skills to robots with different kinematics, degrees of freedom, or camera configurations, the latent space must be re-learned from scratch, requiring expensive data collection and retraining.

Proposed Method: We propose LatentPlan-Transfer, which learns an embodiment-agnostic visual plan latent space by disentangling task-relevant geometric intent (object relations, goal configurations) from embodiment-specific motor primitives. We train a shared multimodal LLM planner across multiple source embodiments using contrastive alignment losses that pull together latents representing the same goal state across different robots. A lightweight embodiment adapter module then translates the shared plan latent into embodiment-specific action conditions via a small set of demonstration-guided fine-tuning examples.

Experiments: (1) Zero-shot transfer from simulation robots (Franka, UR5) to real-world platforms using only 10 target demonstrations. (2) Cross-morphology transfer (arm→bimanual, arm→mobile manipulator) on RLBench and LIBERO benchmarks. (3) Ablations comparing full retraining vs. adapter-only vs. full latent sharing. (4) Visualization of latent alignment across embodiments. We expect 40%+ success improvement over direct fine-tuning baselines in low-data regimes.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction for Multi-Stage Task Planning via Contrastive Visual Latent Decomposition
description: Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, but complex long-horizon tasks (e.g., cooking a meal, assembling furniture) exhibit natural temporal sub-structure with distinct phases. Treating multi-stage tasks with a monolithic latent fails to capture this hierarchy, leading to poor sub-goal tracking and error recovery mid-task. Proposed Method: We extend ThinkAct with a hierarchical temporal decomposition module that segments reasoning plans into K ordered sub-goal latents via contrastive temporal clustering. A learned gating mechanism dynamically selects the active sub-goal latent based on current visual observations and progress estimation, enabling the action model to be conditioned on the appropriate phase-specific plan. We train the decomposition using temporal contrastive loss that enforces ordering constraints (earlier sub-goals dissimilar to later ones) and a phase-boundary detector trained with sparse human-annotated stage labels. A lightweight progress predictor provides curriculum-style reinforcement signals for sub-goal completion. Experiments: (1) CALVIN benchmark with extended 6-step task chains; (2) RLBench multi-stage manipulation tasks; (3) a new cooking simulation benchmark (VirtualKitchen) requiring 8+ sequential sub-tasks; (4) ablations on number of sub-goal latents K and boundary supervision density, measuring sub-goal completion rates and recovery from mid-task failures.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction in Visual Latent Planning for Multi-Stage Manipulation
description: Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, treating the entire task horizon uniformly. This monolithic compression loses temporal structure, making it difficult for the action model to distinguish early-stage sub-goals from late-stage ones, especially in long-horizon tasks with distinct sequential phases (e.g., grasp→transport→assemble→verify). Method: We propose TemporalThink, which decomposes visual plan latents into a hierarchy of temporally-indexed sub-goal latents. A multimodal LLM first generates a structured plan segmented into K discrete stages. Each stage is encoded into a separate visual sub-goal latent via a stage-conditioned VAE. A temporal gating mechanism dynamically selects the active sub-goal latent based on estimated task progress, inferred from proprioceptive state and visual observations. We train the system using a multi-stage reinforcement signal with per-stage completion rewards and smooth transition bonuses that penalize premature or delayed stage transitions. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) CALVIN benchmark extended with 6-stage manipulation tasks, (2) RLBench long-horizon sequences (>10 steps), and (3) real-robot assembly tasks requiring precise sequential coordination. We compare against ThinkAct and ablations removing temporal indexing or gating, measuring task completion rate, stage-transition accuracy, and recovery from mid-task perturbations.

title: HierarchicalThink: Temporally Abstracted Visual Latent Planning with Subgoal Discovery for Long-Horizon Manipulation
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning into a single visual plan latent, but complex long-horizon tasks (e.g., multi-stage kitchen assembly, 10+ step manipulation) require hierarchical temporal abstraction where intermediate subgoals must be dynamically discovered and revised mid-execution. A flat latent representation struggles to capture this multi-level structure.

Proposed Method: We introduce HierarchicalThink, which extends ThinkAct's dual-system with a three-level hierarchy: (1) a goal-level LLM planner that decomposes task instructions into ordered subgoal descriptions, (2) a subgoal discovery module using vector-quantized visual latents to represent discrete waypoints learned via offline trajectory clustering, and (3) a low-level reactive controller conditioned on the current subgoal latent. Reinforcement learning trains the subgoal sequencer using a shaped reward combining subgoal completion, temporal efficiency, and semantic consistency via CLIP-based alignment. A lightweight replanning trigger detects execution failures via visual state divergence and invokes selective subgoal revision without full replanning.

Experiments: (1) CALVIN benchmark with extended 10-task sequences; (2) RLBench long-horizon suite; (3) real Franka arm on multi-stage assembly tasks; (4) ablations comparing flat vs. hierarchical latents, fixed vs. dynamic subgoal counts, and replanning frequency. Baseline comparisons against ThinkAct, SuSIE, and UniPi.

title: HierarchicalThink: Multi-Granularity Visual Latent Planning via Temporal Abstraction for Long-Horizon Manipulation
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning into a single visual plan latent, which struggles to capture the hierarchical structure of complex long-horizon tasks (e.g., cooking, assembly) where both coarse task-level goals and fine-grained skill-level sub-goals must be maintained simultaneously across dozens of steps. A flat latent representation conflates these abstraction levels, causing drift in extended rollouts.

Proposed Method: We introduce HierarchicalThink, which extends the visual latent planning paradigm with a two-level latent hierarchy. A slow-thinking module generates a coarse task-level visual latent updated every K steps, capturing global goal structure. A fast-thinking module generates fine-grained skill-level latents at every step, conditioned on the slow latent. Both are trained with separate RL reward signals: the slow module receives sparse goal-completion rewards, while the fast module receives dense trajectory-consistency and subgoal-reaching rewards. A learned gating mechanism dynamically controls when the slow plan should be revised based on detected environmental discontinuities.

Experiments: We evaluate on (1) CALVIN long-horizon benchmark with 5+ chained tasks, (2) RLBench multi-stage manipulation tasks, and (3) a new cooking simulation environment requiring 20+ sequential steps. We measure success rate, plan coherence over time, and adaptation speed under mid-task perturbations, comparing against ThinkAct and flat-latent baselines.

title: HierarchicalThink: Multi-Granularity Visual Latent Planning with Temporal Abstraction for Open-World Manipulation
description:
Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning plans into a single visual plan latent, treating all task horizons uniformly. This flattened representation struggles when tasks require reasoning at multiple temporal scales simultaneously (e.g., high-level strategy over minutes, mid-level subtask sequencing over seconds, low-level motor primitives over milliseconds). A single latent bottleneck cannot efficiently encode this hierarchical structure, limiting generalization to novel long-horizon tasks.

Proposed Method: We introduce HierarchicalThink, extending ThinkAct with a three-level visual latent hierarchy. A multimodal LLM generates plans at three granularities: goal-level (abstract task decomposition), subtask-level (sequential milestone states), and primitive-level (immediate action affordances). Each level produces a separate visual plan latent via dedicated compression encoders. A hierarchical conditioning mechanism propagates latents top-down to a cascade of action models, where higher-level latents gate lower-level execution. Reinforcement learning rewards operate at each granularity independently, with temporal discount structures aligned to each planning horizon. Level-specific consistency rewards penalize contradictions across abstraction layers.

Experiments: We evaluate on CALVIN benchmark (long-horizon manipulation), RLBench multi-stage tasks, and a new Open-World Kitchen dataset requiring 15+ step manipulation. Ablations isolate contributions of each hierarchy level. We compare against ThinkAct, SayCan, and flat VLA baselines on few-shot generalization to unseen task combinations.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction in Visual Latent Planning for Non-Stationary Embodied Environments
description:
Problem: ThinkAct generates visual plan latents conditioned on current observations, but in non-stationary environments (e.g., dynamic obstacles, changing lighting, moving humans), the compressed latent plan becomes stale within a few execution steps, causing cascading failures during long-horizon tasks. Existing VLA frameworks lack mechanisms to detect when a plan is no longer viable and re-plan at appropriate temporal granularities.

Proposed Method: TemporalThink introduces a hierarchical temporal abstraction layer on top of ThinkAct's dual-system architecture. We add a lightweight 'plan staleness detector' — a small transformer trained via contrastive learning to compare the evolving visual observations against the frozen plan latent, outputting a divergence score. When divergence exceeds a learned threshold, the system triggers selective re-planning at different abstraction levels (micro: replan last sub-goal; macro: replan full trajectory). The multimodal LLM is fine-tuned with temporally-discounted reinforcement rewards that penalize unnecessary re-planning while rewarding timely adaptation. Plan latents are updated incrementally via momentum-based interpolation rather than full regeneration, reducing computational overhead.

Experiments: (1) ALFRED benchmark with injected mid-episode perturbations; (2) RLBench dynamic manipulation tasks with moving distractor objects; (3) Real-robot pick-and-place under human interference. Metrics: task success rate, re-planning frequency, latency overhead, and adaptation speed compared to ThinkAct and reactive baselines.

title: HierarchicalThink: Temporal Abstraction in Visual Latent Planning via Options-Guided Reinforcement for Multi-Stage Manipulation
description: Problem: ThinkAct generates a single visual plan latent conditioning action execution, but complex long-horizon tasks (e.g., multi-object assembly, household chores) require temporally structured sub-goals with variable durations and conditional branching. A flat latent plan cannot efficiently represent hierarchical task decomposition or recover from mid-task failures at the correct abstraction level. Proposed Method: We introduce HierarchicalThink, extending ThinkAct with a two-level visual latent planning architecture inspired by options framework in hierarchical RL. A high-level multimodal LLM decomposes tasks into a sequence of sub-goal visual latents (options), each with a learned termination condition and intrinsic reward. A mid-level planner selects and sequences these options while a low-level action model executes within each option. We train the hierarchy end-to-end using a composite reward: sparse task completion, option-level visual consistency rewards (measuring sub-goal achievement via CLIP similarity), and temporal coherence penalties for premature option termination. Crucially, each option maintains its own compressed visual latent, enabling targeted re-planning when individual sub-goals fail without replanning the entire trajectory. Experiments: We evaluate on CALVIN long-horizon benchmark (5+ step chains), RLBench multi-stage tasks, and a new benchmark requiring conditional branching based on intermediate outcomes. We measure success rate, replanning efficiency after perturbations, and few-shot generalization to novel task orderings compared to flat ThinkAct and non-hierarchical VLA baselines.

title: AdaptThink: Online Plan Latent Refinement via Execution Feedback for Continual Robot Adaptation
description: Problem: ThinkAct compresses reasoning into visual plan latents at inference time but treats these latents as static once generated—when the robot encounters unexpected perturbations (object slippage, occlusion, dynamic obstacles), the plan latent becomes stale and the action model executes a misaligned strategy without self-updating the latent representation. Existing self-correction in ThinkAct relies on replanning from scratch rather than efficient incremental latent refinement. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptThink, an online latent refinement loop that continuously updates the visual plan latent during execution using a lightweight delta-encoder trained via contrastive execution feedback. At each timestep, proprioceptive and visual observations are compared against the expected trajectory encoded in the plan latent; discrepancies above a learned threshold trigger a low-cost gradient-free latent correction using a retrieval-augmented library of failure-recovery sub-plan embeddings. A secondary RL signal based on mid-execution progress rewards shapes the delta-encoder to produce semantically coherent corrections rather than arbitrary latent shifts. Experiments: We evaluate on Meta-World with injected perturbations, FurnitureBench long-horizon assembly with mid-task disturbances, and a real Franka arm setup. Metrics include task success under perturbation, number of full replan calls, and latency overhead compared to ThinkAct baseline.

title: LatentPlan Transfer: Cross-Embodiment Generalization via Shared Visual Plan Representations
description: Problem: While ThinkAct demonstrates that visual plan latents effectively bridge reasoning and action execution within a single robot platform, these compressed latent representations are typically embodiment-specific, requiring full retraining when transferring to new robot morphologies (e.g., from a 6-DOF arm to a mobile manipulator or humanoid). This severely limits scalability across diverse robot fleets. Proposed Method: We propose LatentPlan Transfer, which learns a universal visual plan latent space shared across multiple embodiments by introducing a cross-embodiment alignment objective. During training, an embodiment-agnostic plan encoder maps multimodal LLM reasoning outputs into a shared latent space, while embodiment-specific decoders translate these shared latents into executable actions for each target platform. We use contrastive alignment losses to ensure that semantically equivalent plans (same goal, different robot) cluster together in latent space, combined with a domain-adversarial discriminator to remove embodiment-specific features. A lightweight adapter trained on minimal target-embodiment demonstrations enables rapid transfer. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) cross-embodiment transfer benchmarks using Meta-World and ManiSkill3 with 4+ robot morphologies, (2) zero-shot and few-shot (5-20 demos) transfer success rates, (3) latent space visualization to confirm semantic clustering, and (4) ablations on adapter size versus transfer performance tradeoffs.

title: TemporalThink: Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction in Visual Latent Planning for Multi-Stage Manipulation via Skill-Level Reinforcement
description: Problem: ThinkAct generates reasoning plans as single compressed latents, losing temporal structure for tasks requiring distinct sequential skill phases (e.g., grasp→transport→assemble→verify). This flat representation conflates sub-task boundaries, making it difficult to replan mid-task when individual stages fail. Proposed Method: TemporalThink introduces a hierarchical visual latent planner that decomposes task execution into K discrete skill segments, each represented by a separate visual plan latent. A multimodal LLM first segments the task into named skill phases with predicted durations, then generates per-phase visual latents via a learned temporal encoder. A skill-boundary detector monitors execution progress and triggers replanning at segment transitions using lightweight observation-conditioned updates. Reinforcement learning operates at two levels: a task-level reward for overall goal completion and skill-level shaped rewards for sub-goal achievement, enabling credit assignment across long horizons. The action model conditions on the currently active skill latent, switching latents at predicted boundaries. Experiments: Evaluate on RLBench multi-stage tasks (10+ steps), FurnitureBench assembly sequences, and LIBERO long-horizon benchmarks. Measure per-stage success rates, replanning frequency, and comparison against ThinkAct and flat-latent baselines under mid-task perturbations and novel skill orderings.

title: HierarchicalThink: Temporally Abstracted Visual Latent Planning via Option-Conditioned Reasoning for Multi-Stage Manipulation
description:
Problem: ThinkAct generates reasoning plans as flat sequences, struggling with tasks requiring hierarchical decomposition into reusable sub-skills (e.g., open drawer → grasp object → place in container). A single latent plan vector inadequately captures the compositional structure of long-horizon tasks with discrete phase transitions.

Proposed Method: We introduce HierarchicalThink, which extends ThinkAct's dual-system framework with a three-level hierarchy. A meta-reasoner LLM decomposes tasks into temporally abstract options (sub-goals), each option generates its own visual plan latent via ThinkAct-style reinforced planning, and a low-level controller executes primitive actions conditioned on the active option latent. We train option boundaries using a learned termination critic that detects sub-goal completion from visual observations, rewarded via sparse goal-state matching and inter-option transition smoothness. Options are represented as reusable latent prototypes stored in a retrieval memory, enabling compositional generalization to novel task combinations.

Experiments: (1) LIBERO benchmark suite comparing flat vs. hierarchical latent planning on 10-step+ manipulation sequences; (2) RLBench multi-stage tasks measuring sample efficiency and transfer to unseen task compositions; (3) ablation on option granularity and memory retrieval mechanisms; (4) few-shot adaptation to novel task graphs using composed option prototypes, measuring success rate vs. ThinkAct baseline.
